...comes to an end. A hymn (pad) relating to this illustration has been given in order to make guru and sadguru understood. Further, in order to show guru and sadguru as one and the same, a special exposition has been given in this chapter, Nitya Pralay (Daily Dissolution).

Nitya Pralay

The Example of Shurpanakha — The States of Daily Dissolution and Great Dissolution

As an illustration of how guru and sadguru are counted as one in this matter: at Panchavati, Shurpanakha came to seek Ram in marriage, having come there in a deceitful disguise; from this it was known that she was a rakshasi (demoness), yet in her own mind there was no deceit — she had come with a pure mind. What follows is the teaching of guru-dharma, in the words of Gurua Ganpati's raas.

_Ramakuli nishachari aavi | Shurpankha Lakshmane sambhaavi ||
Shravan naakshikaa chhedyaan | Hari Hari ||_

(The demoness enamored of Ram came; Lakshman took note of Shurpanakha. Her ears and nose he cut off — Hari, Hari.)

When the lust-stricken demoness Shurpanakha came to seek him in marriage, Lakshman cut off her nose and ears.

In this way Ram gave her the teaching of guru-dharma, and so became her guru. Later, in the Krishna incarnation, in Mathuraji, that same woman had to marry the Lord of Grace as Kubja — that was her attaining a sadguru. When she touched the sacred body (vigraha) of Shri Krishna Paramatma, at that very moment she was freed from all worldly desires and, in a state of utterly pure feeling, attained fixity in her own true self (swaatma-nishtha); thus, in the form of Krishna, she attained her sadguru.

Thus, through these words [unclear — a phrase referring back to the earlier doha on 'first recognition of the guru' could not be rendered with confidence from the source], the concept of guru and sadguru has been conveyed. [unclear — the following clause, concerning 'the wheel, the body, and the daughter born to the father,' could not be rendered with confidence from the source] — its hidden meaning being surat-nirat (indrawn attention). This pad has been presented in order to make guru and sadguru known as one.

In this very incarnation, the lust-driven Shurpanakha first made Ram her guru, but Ram did not accept her; in the next incarnation, Krishna married that same Shurpanakha, who had by then come as Kubja. Hence it is said that the lust-driven Shurpanakha, taking God as her chosen husband, held toward him a strong and innocent devotion; because of this, Shurpanakha became infatuated with Ram, and even though she died, her longing and her indrawn attention (surat) to marry him remained unfulfilled. So, when she was born as Kubja, God then spins the thread of her desires and, turning us round in that very wheel of birth and rebirth, grants a new birth in another place, and so fulfills those unfulfilled desires. Such is the turning wheel (rehatmala) by which this happens. Hence, if one's indrawn attention (surat) is fixed upon the guru, then, even in another birth, that same guru comes to one, having become a sadguru.
